scenes.text: This is a fish. I bought it in Oymyakon, often called the coldest permanently inhabited place on Earth. Roughly five hundred people live there. Why would anyone choose that?

I didn't go as a tourist. I went to move in. I packed a toothbrush, a scarf, and a paper map. The map was upside down for most of the trip. My plan was simple. Find the chilliest village anyone has heard of, live there, and get famous for being cold. By the end of the trip, I knew why people really live there. It isn't the cold. It's something that refused to be cold. I also knew whether I was unpacking.

Getting there took a while. I opened my journal to a blank map and drew the route. First a plane. Then a very long drive. Then more of the drive. On paper, it's one short dotted line. In real life, the dotted line has opinions. My backpack didn't fit under the seat, so it sat on my lap, and I sat under it. Outside the window, snow went by. Then more snow. Then a very small sign.

I arrived in late December. Around then, the sun is up for only about four and a half hours a day. I arrived during one of the hours it wasn't. January averages around minus forty-six Celsius. That's about minus fifty-one Fahrenheit. The sign at the edge of the village was very small. So was the village. I stepped out to take a photo of the sign. My eyelashes froze. I didn't know I had eyelashes. My camera took one look at the weather and switched itself off.

Standing by that tiny sign, I had a question. Why is there a village here at all? Somebody picked this spot, on purpose. I had guesses. My first guess was the view. It was dark. My second guess was fishing. I tapped the river with a stick. The river tapped back. My third guess was that nobody checked the weather before moving in. I liked my third guess. My third guess was wrong.

Turns out the answer was hiding in the name. Oymyakon is usually explained as meaning water that does not freeze. Linguists argue about the roots. Some sources trace the word to the Even language, while others point to Sakha. But the story told about this valley is the same. Nearby there were warm springs, water that stayed open through the winter. So I went looking for one. I walked past it twice. It was steaming. I was reading my map. My map was upside down.

Picture a single gas station on an empty highway, at night, in a blizzard. You don't stop there because it's pretty. Reindeer herders stopped at the springs to water their animals and rest before long journeys. If you move reindeer across a frozen landscape, open water isn't a curiosity. It's the whole point. A stopping place became a regular camp. Over time, the camp grew into a permanent village. So the village didn't appear despite the cold. It appeared because, in the middle of all that cold, something refused to freeze. I dipped my water bottle into the spring. For once, it sloshed.

Next, I went to find the chilliest spot in town. That was the whole point of the move. Oymyakon has a monument for it, the Pole of Cold, so I stood next to it and tried to look famous. Why a monument? Because the record that made Oymyakon famous came from the local weather station in nineteen thirty-three. On the sixth of February, it recorded about minus sixty-eight degrees Celsius. That's about minus ninety Fahrenheit. Guinness World Records lists it as minus sixty-seven point seven. The World Meteorological Organization lists minus sixty-seven point eight. So even the number comes with an argument. Either way, it's the lowest temperature on record for a place where people live all year. Well. Almost. Far to the northwest, the town of Verkhoyansk has its own reading from eighteen ninety-two, of about the same number. Some sources say the two towns share the record. Others treat the Verkhoyansk reading as disputed. I measured the distance on my map with my fingers. I decided Verkhoyansk could keep its half.

Then it got complicated. The weather station behind that famous number isn't in Oymyakon itself. It sits in a valley between Oymyakon and a neighbouring village called Tomtor, near Tomtor's airfield. The station and the airfield both date from the Soviet era. Some sources argue that Tomtor, not Oymyakon, is the real Pole of Cold. Oymyakon, meanwhile, has the official monument. So a village got famous partly because someone finally put a thermometer nearby. Thermometers are very good at making places famous. I went to the station. Then back to the monument. Then I tried standing exactly halfway, so I could live in both. Halfway turned out to be mostly frozen road.

Lying on that road, I finally asked a better question. Why is it this cold here at all? Oymyakon isn't even inside the Arctic Circle. It sits a few degrees of latitude south of it. The reason is boring and brilliant. In winter, a huge, stable zone of high pressure called the Siberian High settles over this part of Asia. It brings clear, dry skies, and clear skies let the ground lose its heat straight up into space. Then there's the valley. Cold air is heavy. It slides downhill and pools on the valley floor, like water in a bowl, while the mountains around it keep warmer air out. Researchers measuring this valley have found the mountain slopes above it can be far warmer in winter than the valley floor. So the cold isn't a spot. It's the whole bowl. I thought about climbing out. Up there it's warmer. Up there it's also a mountain. I stayed in the bowl.

I'm going to put the fish down for this part. The same era brought something much darker to this region. In the nineteen thirties, the Soviet Union built a network of forced labour camps across the Kolyma region, part of the Gulag system, largely to mine gold. Prisoners began building the Kolyma Highway in the early nineteen thirties, and forced labour continued on it into the nineteen fifties. Many of them did not survive. The village's story begins with the springs. But the highway that crosses this region was built by people who had no choice.

Back in the village, I tried to get through one ordinary day. Morning. Still dark. Outside, a car sat in the street with its engine running and nobody in it. Cars are often left running for hours, or warmed with a fire before starting, because a frozen engine may refuse to start at all. Think of your car on a winter morning. Now imagine the winter never gives back the keys. I patted the car on the hood, like a horse. The car kept running. It had places to be.

Midday, I went to the market. Food here comes mostly from animals and the river: meat, and fish that in winter is sold frozen solid and stacked like firewood. Farming in frozen ground is close to impossible. I asked for a bag. The fish did not need a bag. The fish could stand up on its own. That's when it clicked. In winter, the village itself is the freezer. I carried my fish home on my shoulder, like a plank. Yes. This fish.

Afternoon. I needed a bathroom. Beneath the surface the ground is permafrost, frozen all year, which makes ordinary water pipes very hard to keep working. Many homes use outdoor toilets. I looked at the path to the outhouse for a long time. I made a decision. I waited. On the way back, I passed the school. According to Russian news reports, younger pupils in the district get the day off when it reaches around minus fifty-two. The exact cut-off for each age group depends on who you ask. Plenty of schools elsewhere close for a light dusting of snow. I asked whether Oymyakon has snow days. It does. They're just extremely specific.

Evening. I made tea to warm up. The tea did not warm up. It grew a thin, shiny skin and gave up. I sat by the window with my scarf, my upside-down map, and a fish that was clearly handling this better than me. The fish had made peace with everything. I had not. That night, I started packing.

And yet, I went back in July. Partly out of stubbornness. Mostly to see whether the village had a second personality. It does. I'd just missed the long days. By late June, daylight lasts more than twenty hours. In July twenty ten, the station recorded thirty-four point six degrees Celsius. That's about ninety-four Fahrenheit. Put the record low and the record high side by side, and the gap is roughly one hundred and two degrees. Very few places on Earth have record highs and lows that far apart. I had packed the same bag. Everything in it was fur. And for one sweaty afternoon, I wanted to move in again.

Then I met the residents who never go inside. Yakutian horses live outdoors all year in this region, right through the winter. A genetic study published in twenty fifteen found that they descend from domestic horses brought here only a few centuries ago. They adapted to the cold remarkably fast, with compact bodies and very thick winter coats. Imagine buying the right jacket, except your body grows the jacket for you. My only adaptation is a large backpack. I tried to make friends with one. The horse kept eating. The horse has seen tourists before.

I had also missed the party. Every spring, the district hosts a festival called the Pole of Cold, with events in villages including Oymyakon and Tomtor. Its star is Chyskhaan, the Sakha Lord of Cold, who reportedly has his own ice residence. In twenty twenty-five, there was even a marathon here. In the cold. On purpose. So the water brought the herders, the thermometer brought the fame, and now the cold itself brings visitors. A village that grew up around water that wouldn't freeze now welcomes people because of everything that does.

So here's what my desk knows now. The cold was never the reason to come. It was the price of staying. Would I move there? The springs are lovely. The summer surprised me. But the winters are long, dark and brutally cold, and I lasted about one cup of tea. My verdict is NOPE. That valley is for people who grew up with it, or who truly love winter: silence, clear skies, and a summer that feels earned. The fish lives in my freezer now. It's the warmest winter it has ever had. One January there, for one July. Would you take that trade?
